newsitem.title: USA: U.S. swears in first post-war envoy to Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: U.S. swears in first post-war envoy to Vietnam.

text.p: Former Representative Douglas "Pete" Peterson, a fighter pilot who spent 6-1/2 years as a prisoner of war in Hanoi, was sworn in on Tuesday as the first U.S. ambassador to post-war Vietnam vowing to build a bridge across a "river of pain."

Before taking the oath of office from Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Peterson said he planned to devote much of his time to healing still-open wounds of a war that ended with the Communist victory over U.S.-backed forces in 1975.

"I would hope that my example would lead some to rethink their positions," he told Reuters on Monday, citing Americans who oppose closer ties because of 2,127 U.S. servicemen still listed as missing from the war, 1,588 of them in Vietnam.

"And I hope and pray that we will be able to bridge this river of pain that exists between these two cultures," he said of the United States and Vietnam. "And I'm going to devote a major part of my activities in Vietnam to doing just that."

Peterson, who served six years in the House of Representatives as a Florida Democrat, began his involvement with Vietnam 31 years ago as a Thailand-based U.S. Air Force fighter pilot. On Sept. 10, 1966, on his 67th mission, his aircraft was shot down near Hanoi and he was a prisoner until his repatriation in March 1973.

In the interview at the State Department, Peterson said the strengthening of U.S. ties with Vietnam, normalised in July 1995, continued to hinge on Hanoi's help in providing the fullest possible accounting for missing Americans.

"As we move forward with that issue and that level of cooperation then we'll be able to move in to other areas of mutual concern," said Peterson, who was to arrive in Hanoi on May 9 after stops in Hawaii, headquarters of U.S. forces in the Pacific, and in Bangkok.
He described possible future port calls to Vietnam by U.S. Navy ships as a "logical" extension of nascent military exchanges, but added: "We are not trying to move ahead aggressively in this area."

"There is a great deal of credibility that has to be established on both sides here," he said. "On the economic fronts, the human rights fronts, on the POW-MIA issue, on science and technology, environment, narcotics -- all of those things, really at this juncture, have a priority."

He added: "To be brutally honest, I think that there is a good deal of suspicion on the part of the military in Vietnam as to anything we may wish to go forth on with the Vietnamese, and there is no reason to raise that level of sensitivity."

Possible port calls to Vietnam are also a sensitive matter in U.S. relations with China, an historic foe of Vietnam. Washington is trying to build more stable ties with Beijing despite tension over human rights, arms proliferation concerns and strains over Taiwan, Tibet and Hong Kong.

U.S. Ambassador to China James Sasser said recently that he expected Beijing to "swallow" any future U.S. port calls to Vietnam. "They may not love it but they can swallow it," he told Reuters on March 6 at the Freedom Forum's First Amendment Centre at Vanderbilt University in Nashville, Tennessee.

Peterson said economic normalisation with Vietnam may be further off than he had projected in his Senate confirmation testimony in February, when he said he expected negotiations on a trade treaty to be completed "sometime later this year."

He told Reuters completion this year of such a treaty, which would require House and Senate approval, was the "most optimistic scenario" and that the matter could drag on. He said the United States was awaiting Hanoi's reply to a U.S. draft treaty that would improve the business climate by cutting tariffs, ending export licenses and simplifying government approvals.
